content: Tinea capitis is a fungal infection that affects the scalp. It is also commonly referred to as ringworm of the scalp. Symptoms of Tinea Capitis: Tinea capitis can involve either specific areas of the scalp or the entire scalp. Infected areas often appear bald with small black dots, which are caused by hair that has broken off. The skin in these areas may be round, scaly, red, or swollen (inflamed). In some cases, pus-filled sores known as kerions may develop. Additional symptoms can include a low-grade fever (approximately 100–101°F) and swollen lymph nodes in the neck. Itching of the scalp is a common symptom. Causes of Tinea Capitis: Fungi are microorganisms that can live on dead tissue, such as that found in hair, nails, and the outer layers of skin. The body naturally hosts a variety of fungi, but tinea capitis is specifically caused by mold-like fungi called dermatophytes. These fungi thrive in warm, moist environments. Factors that increase the likelihood of developing a tinea infection include minor injuries to the skin or scalp, poor hygiene, and prolonged wetness of the skin (e.g., from sweating). Risk Factors: Tinea capitis, or ringworm, is highly contagious and can spread easily to others. It most commonly affects children and often resolves on its own after puberty, though it can occur at any age. The infection can be transmitted through direct contact with an infected person’s skin or by touching contaminated items such as combs, hats, or clothing. Pets, particularly cats, can also spread the infection. Diagnosis: A healthcare provider may suspect tinea capitis based on the appearance of the scalp. A diagnostic tool called a Wood’s lamp may be used to identify a fungal scalp infection. Additionally, the provider may take a swab of the affected area and send it for a fungal culture, though results can take up to three weeks. In rare cases, a skin biopsy of the scalp may be performed. When to Seek Medical Care: If you experience symptoms of tinea capitis, it is important to schedule an appointment with a healthcare provider. Home remedies are not effective in treating this condition. Treatment Options: Treatment for tinea capitis involves taking oral antifungal medications prescribed by a healthcare provider. Common medications include griseofulvin, terbinafine, and itraconazole. These medications are typically taken for 4 to 8 weeks. It is also important to keep the affected area clean. Using a medicated shampoo containing ketoconazole or selenium sulfide may help slow or prevent the spread of the infection through airborne transmission, but shampoo alone cannot eliminate the infection. Other family members and pets should be examined and treated if necessary. For example: Children in the household may use the medicated shampoo 2 to 3 times per week for approximately 6 weeks. Adults only need to use the shampoo if they show signs of tinea capitis or ringworm. Once treatment begins, additional hygiene measures should be taken: Wash towels in warm, soapy water and dry them thoroughly after each use by an infected individual. Soak combs and brushes in a mixture of half bleach and half water for 1 hour daily for 3 days. Avoid sharing combs, hairbrushes, hats, towels, pillowcases, or helmets with others in the household. Prognosis: Tinea capitis can be challenging to treat and may recur after treatment. However, in many cases, the condition resolves on its own when the individual reaches puberty.
